strengths: The paper proposes a simple and plausible dataset distillation pipeline: compute per-class Wasserstein barycenters in a pretrained feature space, then recover images with feature and per-class BatchNorm-statistics matching.
The empirical results are strong on large/high-resolution settings, including ImageNet-1K, with sizeable gains over several reported scalable distillation baselines across IPC budgets.

The paper includes useful supporting evidence: ablations for Wasserstein vs. CE-style feature losses and PCBN vs. standard BN, cross-architecture transfer, runtime/memory comparisons, hyperparameter sensitivity, and qualitative visualizations.
Reproducibility is helped by code availability and reasonably detailed implementation/hyperparameter descriptions in the supplement.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. Much of the system builds on known components: pretrained-feature inversion, BN-statistics regularization, FKD/relabeling, and standard free-support Wasserstein barycenter computation. The main contribution is an effective combination rather than a fundamentally new distillation paradigm.

The theoretical justification is weak relative to the claims. The appendix analyzes W1 loss bounds under strong assumptions, while the implemented method uses feature-space barycenters with squared Euclidean costs; the discussion of MMD also partly compares against simplified mean-matching variants rather than the strongest characteristic-kernel alternatives.

The baseline comparison is not fully controlled. Several table entries are taken from reported results with missing error bars or missing IPC settings, and not all strong baselines appear to be rerun under exactly the same training, augmentation, teacher, and FKD protocol.

The MMD comparison is not entirely satisfying: direct replacement gives near-random performance, while the “vanilla” comparison removes engineering tricks from both methods. This helps isolate the metric but does not establish that Wasserstein is superior to well-tuned modern MMD-based distillation pipelines.

The efficiency and practical-impact claims should be qualified because the method requires training a full-data teacher model before distillation; the benefit is strongest when the distilled set or teacher can be reused, not necessarily when counting the entire end-to-end cost for a single training run.

Empirical results are strong across ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K, with especially compelling gains at 10/50/100 IPC and performance close to full-data training in some high-IPC settings.

The method appears practical: it is simple to implement on top of scalable distribution-matching pipelines, has modest additional runtime over SRe2L-style approaches, and provides implementation details and code availability.
The paper is generally clear and well motivated, with useful connections to optimal transport and a reasonable discussion of societal impact.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental relative to recent ImageNet-scale distillation pipelines: the method relies heavily on a pretrained teacher, feature inversion/recovery, BatchNorm-statistic regularization, and FKD-style training, so the independent contribution of Wasserstein barycenters versus pipeline engineering could be separated more sharply.

The theoretical justification is suggestive rather than rigorous. The paper often frames the objective as a Wasserstein barycenter problem, but in the single-distribution per-class case it is closer to Wasserstein quantization/projection; the downstream generalization claims are not theoretically established.

The comparison to MMD is not fully satisfying. The direct replacement reportedly gives near-random performance, while the controlled comparison removes many engineering components; the supplementary argument also contrasts Wasserstein with mean/linear-kernel matching more than with strong characteristic-kernel MMD methods.

Experimental fairness has some residual ambiguity because several baselines are taken from reported numbers, some lack error bars, and it is not always clear that teacher training, feature extraction, barycenter computation, FKD, and evaluation protocols are included consistently in runtime and accuracy comparisons.

The evaluation is mostly centered on ResNet-18 as the distillation teacher and ImageNet-style classification. More evidence across teacher architectures, weaker teachers, additional datasets, and non-classification/robustness/privacy settings would better support the broad claims about applicability.

strengths: Addresses an important dataset distillation problem at ImageNet-scale, where efficiency and high-resolution performance are genuinely valuable to computer vision practice.

The proposed combination of feature-space Wasserstein support points and per-class BatchNorm statistics is simple, scalable, and empirically effective, with strong reported gains on ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K across several IPC budgets.

The paper includes useful evidence beyond the main table: cross-architecture transfer, runtime/memory measurements, ablations for the Wasserstein loss and PCBN, sensitivity studies, and visualizations of synthetic diversity.
Reproducibility is helped by a code link, implementation details, hyperparameters, and a discussion of social impact and bias/efficiency tradeoffs.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate: the core objective with a single empirical distribution is closer to free-support quantization/k-means in pretrained feature space than a general Wasserstein barycenter contribution, and this connection is not fully acknowledged or analyzed.

Some comparisons are not fully controlled. Many baseline results are taken from prior reports, CDA lacks error bars, and it is unclear whether all methods share identical augmentation, relabeling/FKD, evaluation, and tuning protocols.

The MMD comparison is not decisive: the paper notes that direct replacement gives near-random results, then compares stripped-down variants. This makes the claim that Wasserstein itself is the main cause of improvement less isolated from PCBN, teacher features, FKD, and other engineering choices.

The theoretical appendix provides intuition rather than a strong justification; it relies on broad Lipschitz/RKHS assumptions and mainly critiques linear-kernel mean matching, which does not fully establish superiority of the proposed metric in the actual deep feature optimization setting.

Efficiency analysis is limited to ImageNette 1 IPC and appears to exclude important costs such as teacher training/squeezing and possibly parts of barycenter computation; scaling costs on ImageNet-1K and larger IPC settings would make the practical claim stronger.

The method depends heavily on a pretrained classifier and inherited SRe2L/FKD-style stages, but ablations on teacher architecture, feature extractor quality, use of learned weights during downstream training, and removal of FKD are limited or absent.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and practically motivated dataset distillation method: compute class-wise Wasserstein free-support prototypes in a pretrained feature space, then recover synthetic images with feature matching plus per-class BatchNorm statistics. The method is simple, scalable, and well aligned with current large-scale distillation pipelines.

Empirical results are strong on high-resolution benchmarks. WMDD improves substantially over recent scalable methods on Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet-1K, including large gains at 10/50/100 IPC, and the cross-architecture study shows useful transfer beyond the ResNet-18 distillation backbone.

The ablations are meaningful: the paper separates the effects of Wasserstein feature matching and PCBN, studies alternative metrics including sliced Wasserstein, tests regularization strength and feature-layer choice, and provides qualitative visualizations that support the claimed increase in diversity.

The manuscript is generally readable and gives enough implementation detail to understand the pipeline, with code promised and supplementary hyperparameters included. The social-impact discussion is appropriate for this type of efficiency-oriented work.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than deep. The method is largely a combination of known components: pretrained-feature recovery as in SRe2L-style pipelines, optimal-transport free-support barycenters/prototypes, and BatchNorm-statistic regularization. PCBN is a useful engineering contribution, but not conceptually transformative.

The theoretical framing is somewhat loose. The method is described as Wasserstein barycenter computation, but for each class it is effectively approximating a single empirical distribution with a limited-support measure, closer to Wasserstein quantization/prototype learning than a barycenter over multiple distributions. The appendix comparison to MMD relies on broad assumptions and does not tightly justify the actual squared-feature-space objective used in the algorithm.

The baseline comparison has some fairness and completeness concerns. Many baseline numbers are taken from papers, some entries are missing, CDA lacks error bars, and the MMD comparison is acknowledged as hard to make direct. The reported large gains are convincing overall, but a fully controlled reimplementation of the strongest recent baselines under the same FKD/training/evaluation pipeline would strengthen the case.

Efficiency is not fully characterized. The paper emphasizes fast distillation iterations, but the pipeline requires training a full teacher on the real data, and the total cost of squeezing/pretraining, barycenter computation at ImageNet scale, recovery, relabeling/FKD, and evaluation is not comprehensively compared against all baselines.

Some experimental choices need more scrutiny: using 20% of the distilled data as validation for cross-architecture evaluation may reduce comparability; only a limited set of datasets/backbones is studied; and the low-IPC setting is not uniformly strong, with some older methods outperforming WMDD at 1 IPC on ImageNette/Tiny-ImageNet.

Several methodological details remain underspecified in the main paper, including initialization of barycenter supports, exact use of learned weights during downstream training/FKD, and sensitivity to the pretrained teacher quality. These affect reproducibility and interpretation of where the gains come from.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant problem: scalable dataset distillation for high-resolution datasets, including ImageNet-1K.
The method is simple and well motivated: class-wise Wasserstein/OT feature prototypes plus per-class BatchNorm regularization fit naturally into the SRe2L-style pipeline.
Empirical results are strong. Table 1 reports consistent gains over scalable DD baselines across ImageNette, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K, especially at 10/50/100 IPC.

The paper includes useful evidence beyond headline accuracy: cross-architecture transfer, runtime/memory comparison, ablations of Wasserstein loss and PCBN, sliced Wasserstein comparison, layer sensitivity, lambda sensitivity, and visualizations.
Reproducibility is helped by code release, named libraries, reported hyperparameters, repeated runs with error bars for most experiments, and a supplemental implementation section.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: much of the pipeline, including pretrained teacher features, recovery, relabeling/FKD, and BN-statistic regularization, is inherited from prior large-scale DD work; the main changes are the OT feature target and PCBN.

The technical formulation overstates the connection to Wasserstein barycenters. With a single empirical distribution and an m-atom support constraint, the objective is closer to Wasserstein quantization/coreset construction than the standard multi-distribution barycenter problem.

The optimization derivation is not fully rigorous: the position update treats the transport plan as fixed and calls the Hessian 2 w_j I, but the optimal plan is itself a nonsmooth function of the support locations, so convergence/local-optimality claims are stronger than justified.

The theoretical appendix is mostly a standard loss-discrepancy bound and does not convincingly prove Wasserstein superiority; it switches to W1 while the method uses squared Euclidean/W2-style costs, relies on strong assumptions, and does not compare constants meaningfully.

The comparison to MMD is not completely satisfying. The direct MMD replacement gives near-random results, but the “vanilla” comparison removes many engineering components and does not isolate whether the gains come from the metric, PCBN, feature targets, weighting, or the broader training recipe.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete despite the code link: barycenter initialization, exact POT solver choices, subgradient step sizes, use of sample weights during later training/relabeling, augmentation details, and full evaluation schedules are partly deferred to prior work rather than specified fully.

Efficiency evidence is limited: runtime is measured mainly on ImageNette 1 IPC, and the full cost of teacher training plus large-scale per-class OT computation is not clearly accounted for in the practical savings claim.
